generatedProse.concept-context: Passive revision is common in any subject because there is so much to read back over: notes, summaries, chapters and handouts. Reading them again feels productive, but it only builds recognition. Active revision makes you produce the knowledge instead. You recall an idea from memory, explain a concept in your own words, sketch out how something works, or work through a practice problem. That effort of retrieval and application is what an exam actually asks of you.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who sit down to revise the same topic for two hours.

Student A reads through his notes, highlights the key points, and reads them again. By the end the pages look well used and the material feels familiar. But Student A has only recognised it, not produced it. Asked to explain the topic the next day, he can picture the page but cannot quite reconstruct the idea. This is passive review.

Student B reads her notes once, then closes them. She writes out the main idea from memory, checks what she left out, turns the gaps into questions, and answers a short practice question that applies the idea. It feels harder and slower. But the next day she can reproduce the idea and use it, because the effort of retrieving it is what fixed it. This is active revision.

Both students spent two hours. Only Student B made the knowledge retrievable, by recreating and applying it rather than re-reading it.
generatedProse.summary: Active revision beats passive review because it makes you recreate or apply knowledge rather than take it in again. Re-reading your notes builds recognition; recalling an idea, explaining a concept and working practice problems build the retrieval an exam demands. You can now tell the two apart and swap a passive habit for an active one. The next lesson gives you a set of active techniques to choose from.

check.body: In the worked example, what was the active move Student B made instead of re-reading?

items.text: She closed her notes, wrote the main idea from memory, and checked what she had missed.
She read her notes more carefully than Student A did.
She highlighted the key points first.
She spent longer on her notes than Student A did.

feedback.correct: That's right. Writing the idea from memory and checking it is active revision in action.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for the move that made Student B produce the idea, not re-read it.
feedback.incorrectFinal: The active move was to close the notes, write the idea from memory, and check the gaps. Reading more carefully, highlighting or spending longer are all still passive.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; name the cast directly in the prose (the pack supplies the whole body). The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
